title: Dead to Sin, Alive to God
summary: Paul answers the charge that grace encourages sin. Believers were baptized into Christ's death and raised with him to walk in newness of life, so sin no longer has the right to rule them. They are to count themselves dead to sin and alive to God, and to offer their bodies to God as instruments of righteousness. Everyone serves some master; those freed from sin have become slaves of God, and the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus.
story: Chapter 5 ended with a bold claim: where sin increased, grace increased all the more. That invites the objection Paul says his opponents already made (3:8): if grace grows where sin grows, why not keep sinning? Chapter 6 answers it twice, in verses 1-14 and again in verses 15-23, each time beginning with a question and the strong reply “Certainly not!” Paul does not answer by retreating from grace, but by explaining what grace has done. Those who belong to Christ have not merely been forgiven; they have been joined to him in his death and resurrection and brought under a new master. Chapter 7 will turn to the role of the law, and chapter 8 to life in the Spirit.
historical:
Paul writes to a church where baptism was the universal rite of entry into the Christian community, and he assumes his readers know its meaning (“aren't you aware?”). The earliest Christian baptism seems to have been in water, often by immersion, though the New Testament does not describe the mode in detail. Immersion gives force to Paul's picture of being buried with Christ and raised with him, and many interpreters think he had it in mind.

Slavery was everywhere in the Roman world. In the city of Rome a large part of the population were slaves or former slaves, and many members of the Roman church, as the names in chapter 16 suggest, were probably slaves or freedpersons themselves. Slaves could be set free, and a freed slave often remained bound to his former master by obligations. Paul says he is speaking in human terms (verse 19) when he uses the image: freedom from sin is not independence but a change of owner.
cultural:
Several of Paul's images come from daily life in the empire. The word translated instruments in verse 13 (hoplon) usually meant weapons, especially a soldier's arms, so offering the parts of the body to sin or to God is like handing weapons to one side or the other in a war. The word wages in verse 23 (opsonion) was used for a soldier's pay or rations. Sin, Paul says, is a paymaster who pays in death. God does not pay wages at all; he gives a gift (charisma).

The idea of dying to a former life was not unknown in the ancient world. Some mystery religions spoke of initiates sharing the fate of a dying and rising god. Scholars once argued that Paul borrowed from them, but most now think the differences are decisive: Paul's baptism rests on the death and resurrection of a recent historical person, once for all, not on a myth of the seasons, and his roots are in Jewish thought about God's people sharing the destiny of their representative.
literary: The chapter is built from two parallel responses to two similar questions. The first (verses 1-14) uses the language of death and life: died with Christ, buried, raised, newness of life. Its logic moves from what has happened (verses 3-10, indicatives) to what believers must therefore do (verses 11-14, commands): count yourselves, do not let sin reign, present yourselves to God. The second (verses 15-23) uses the language of slavery and freedom, and ends with a sharp contrast of two outcomes: fruit leading to holiness, and death as the end of sin. The final verse, with its balanced lines of wages and gift, death and eternal life, sums up the chapter and in a sense the whole first half of the letter.

outline.t: Baptized into Christ's death, raised to new life
United with Christ: dead to sin, alive to God
Do not let sin reign; present yourselves to God
Slaves of the one you obey
Two masters, two outcomes: death or eternal life

doctrines.note: Salvation includes not only forgiveness but freedom from sin's rule. Believers were united with Christ in his death and resurrection; the old self was crucified with him. The new life that follows is the fruit of grace, not a way of earning it.

Baptism marks union with Christ in his death and resurrection. Christian traditions differ on how: Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, and many Anglican and Reformed Christians hold that God works through baptism to unite the believer to Christ; Baptists and many other evangelicals hold that baptism is a public sign of a union that happens by faith. Some interpreters think Paul is speaking of baptism in the Spirit. All agree that union with Christ is the heart of the matter.
Believers are to present the parts of their bodies to God as instruments of righteousness, bearing fruit that leads to holiness. Christian holiness is embodied and practical, not merely inward.
Sin appears here as a master that reigns, gives orders, and pays wages. People are not neutral; they serve sin or God. The good news is that sin's claim has been broken, even though its pull remains.

words.note: Baptizo, to dip, immerse, or wash. In ordinary Greek it could describe dipping cloth in dye or a ship sinking. In the church it became the name of the rite of entry. Paul says believers were baptized into Christ, into his death, which describes both the rite and the union it signifies.

Sustauroomai, to be crucified with. Paul uses it here and in Galatians 2:20. The old self, the person one was in Adam under sin's rule, was crucified with Christ. Paul speaks of this as something that has happened, not something believers must achieve.

Ephapax, once for all. Christ died to sin once for all; his death cannot be repeated and does not need to be. The same word appears in Hebrews for Christ's single, sufficient sacrifice (Hebrews 7:27, 9:12, 10:10).
Opsonion, wages or rations, especially a soldier's pay. Sin pays what it has earned: death. The contrast with charisma, gift, in the same verse is deliberate. Eternal life is never wages.

christ: Everything in this chapter depends on believers being in Christ. Christ died to sin once for all and was raised, and death no longer has dominion over him. Those united to him share in both events: his death means sin has lost its claim, and his resurrection means they walk in newness of life now and will share his resurrection fully. The phrase in Christ Jesus in verse 11 names the new place a believer lives. Paul does not tell believers to become dead to sin by effort, but to count as true what has already happened in Christ, and then to live accordingly. The chapter ends by naming him as the source of the gift: eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

hard.q: If believers are dead to sin, why do Christians still sin?
hard.a:
Paul says believers died to sin and have been set free from it, yet he commands them not to let sin reign and not to offer their bodies to it. That implies sin still exerts a pull. Interpreters have explained the tension in several ways.

Most read Paul as describing a change of status and of power, not the end of temptation: sin is a dethroned master that still tries to give orders, and believers must now refuse what they once could not. This is sometimes described as the already and not yet: the old order has been broken, but the new has not fully arrived, and the body is still mortal (verse 12). Some holiness traditions, including Wesleyan teaching on entire sanctification, hold that a believer can by grace come to love God so wholly that deliberate sin no longer rules, while still being subject to mistakes and weakness. Reformed and Lutheran traditions stress that sin remains in believers until death, while its dominion is broken. All agree that Paul's command to count yourselves dead to sin rests on something God has done, and that the answer to ongoing sin is not less grace but a deeper grasp of it.

questions: Paul says everyone serves some master. What are the things that tend to give you orders?
What does it mean in practice to count yourself dead to sin and alive to God on an ordinary day?
Why does Paul insist that eternal life is a gift and not a wage? How would thinking of it as a wage change how you live?
